buckets.title: Universal divisibility with consecutive integers
buckets.topic: Number Systems; proposed IMO-style divisibility proof enrichment

conventions.statement: n is an arbitrary positive integer, not a chosen sample.
a divides N means there exists an integer k with N=a*k.
Every integer has exactly one residue modulo m among 0,...,m-1.
A factor of 2 and a factor of 3 in the product may occur in different terms; 2 and 3 are coprime.

capabilities.action: Prove a divisibility statement for every allowed starting integer using exhaustive remainder classes and coprime factors.
capabilities.success_criterion: For all positive integers n, justify that 6 divides n(n+1)(n+2), and independently prove 24 divides n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3), without treating finite examples as a proof.

microtopics.title: Reasoning from exhaustive residue cases to a universal divisibility claim
microtopics.badge_reason: A finite set of examples is not a universal proof; learners must connect parity, exhaustive modular cases and coprime divisibility across an arbitrary starting integer.
entry_assumptions: Positive integer arithmetic and the meaning of a divisor.
Even and odd integers alternate when moving to the next integer.
A positive integer modulo 3 has residue 0, 1 or 2.
If two coprime integers divide a number then so does their product.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Convert finite observations into a universal argument by establishing a guaranteed factor of 2 and a guaranteed factor of 3 within any three consecutive integers, and then use coprimality to conclude divisibility by 6.

teaching_path.action: Let n denote an arbitrary positive starting integer; the three consecutive factors are n, n+1 and n+2.
teaching_path.why_valid: This representation includes every eligible triple, not merely three sampled values.

teaching_path.action: Consider n and n+1: one is even, so the product of the three integers has at least one factor of 2.
teaching_path.why_valid: Parity alternates in adjacent integers. The statement holds for both possible parities of n.

teaching_path.action: Separate n modulo 3 into cases 0, 1 and 2. Identify n, n+2 or n+1 respectively as divisible by 3.
teaching_path.why_valid: These three remainder classes are exhaustive and exactly one member of any three consecutive integers has remainder 0 modulo 3.

teaching_path.action: Combine both divisors: since the whole product is divisible by 2 and 3 and these are coprime, it is divisible by 6.
teaching_path.why_valid: When coprime integers 2 and 3 divide the same whole number, their product 6 also divides that number; we have justified both divisibilities for every n.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Checking a few starting integers proves the divisibility assertion for all future n.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If the starting integer is far larger than every sample you checked, what property guarantees divisibility without recalculation?
misconceptions.repair: Use complete residue cases modulo 2 and 3 to cover all possible starts; identify guaranteed factors and apply the coprime-product rule.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The ending factor t is always divisible by 3, so checking the other two factors is unnecessary.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Try t=4: is t divisible by 3? Which one of t−2, t−1, t is divisible by 3 instead, and what changes when t leaves remainder 0, 1 or 2 modulo 3?
misconceptions.repair: Replace the fixed-factor claim with all three cases: when t mod 3 is 0 use t; when it is 1 use t−1; when it is 2 use t−2. Combine the guaranteed factor of 3 with an even factor using gcd(2,3)=1.

exit_task.prompt: Prove, for every positive integer n, that n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3) is divisible by 24. Give a general proof, not only examples.

answer.summary: The product of four consecutive positive integers is divisible by 24.
reasoning: Write the factors as n, n+1, n+2 and n+3, with n arbitrary and positive.
Exactly one of these four has remainder 0 modulo 4, and another even factor has remainder 2 modulo 4. Their product is divisible by 8.
Within any four consecutive integers there is a multiple of 3, so the full product is divisible by 3.
Because 8 and 3 are coprime, the full product is divisible by 24 for every n.
answer.check: For each remainder n modulo 24, verify the four-factor product is a multiple of 24; this is an independent exhaustive modular check, not a replacement for the proof.

microtopics.research_contribution: Authored reasoning construction with explicit case completeness and coprimality. Curriculum placement, diagrams, learner comprehension, formal product acceptance and source exam representation remain pending.

construction_units.decision: Derive divisibility by 6 from parity and modulo 3 as exhaustive guarantees, not finite examples.

independent_checks.statement: Check the three-factor product modulo 6 for all six integer residue classes.
Check the four-factor exit product modulo 24 for all 24 residue classes.

compact_anchor.prompt: Why must one of three consecutive integers be divisible by 3?
compact_anchor.result: Their residues modulo 3 cycle through 0, 1 and 2, so one remainder must be 0.

predict.prompt: A student checks t=3,4,5 and claims that (t−2)(t−1)t is divisible by 6 for every integer t≥3. Do those three checks PROVE the word every? Begin your written response with yes or no and explain what would count as evidence for every admissible t; then construct the general proof in the same response. If using a printed handout, write on a separate sheet.
predict.defensible_answer: No. Three checks are instances, not an exhaustive proof. A valid argument must establish a guaranteed even factor, a guaranteed multiple-of-three factor and their coprime combination for arbitrary t≥3.

attempt.produces: A general proof for an arbitrary t≥3, including explicit parity, all three modulo-3 cases, the coprime combination, and an explanation of why these exhaustive claims are stronger than examples.

rubric.criterion: State t is an arbitrary integer at least 3 and not just one selected example.
rubric.evidence_of: The variable ranges over every allowed case rather than one sampled case.

rubric.criterion: Prove that one factor is even for any t, naming why adjacent integers suffice.
rubric.evidence_of: A factor of 2 is guaranteed independently of the parity of t.

rubric.criterion: Cover t modulo 3 equal to 0,1,2, showing respectively t, t−1, t−2 divisible by 3.
rubric.evidence_of: One factor of 3 is guaranteed for every allowed residue class; no case omitted.

rubric.criterion: Use gcd(2,3)=1 to conclude 6 divides the whole product, and distinguish proof from examples.
rubric.evidence_of: The two independently guaranteed divisors combine, giving a universal conclusion.

accepted: Let t≥3 be any integer. Among t−1 and t, one is even. If t mod 3 is 0,1,2, then respectively t,t−1,t−2 is divisible by 3. Thus 2 and 3 divide (t−2)(t−1)t; since gcd(2,3)=1, 6 divides it for every allowed t.

Put n=t−2. For every n≥1, n(n+1)(n+2) contains an even factor and a multiple of three by an exhaustive residue argument; coprimality implies a factor of six. Because every allowed t gives an allowed n, the claim follows for all t≥3.
rejected: I tested t=3,4,5 and all gave multiples of six, so the statement is proved.
The factor t is always divisible by 3, so the product is a multiple of 6.

task.prompt: With t any integer at least 3, reconstruct a proof that (t−2)(t−1)t is divisible by 6. Do NOT list sample products as your justification. Show what forces a 2, what forces a 3, and why the two facts combine.
givens: t is an arbitrary integer and t≥3.
The three factors are consecutive and positive.
A universally quantified statement must cover every admissible start.

route.ask: Would proof for three tested t values still cover an untested t? What feature must your answer guarantee instead?
route.why_this_ask: Forces learner to reject empirical sampling before deciding which theorem can be used; not an expert's opening formula.

route.ask: Among the two adjacent factors t−1 and t, can both be odd? What factor must appear, regardless of t's parity?
route.why_this_ask: Elicits unavoidable factor two with a falsifiable parity question, rather than stating that a factor exists.

route.ask: Suppose t leaves remainder 0,1 or 2 on division by 3. Which of t, t−1, t−2 is then divisible by 3 in each case?
route.why_this_ask: The learner has to supply all three exclusive cases and choose the matching factor; this is the protected mathematical crux.

route.ask: If 2 and 3 might divide DIFFERENT factors, what can be concluded about the integer product and why does gcd(2,3)=1 matter?
route.why_this_ask: Prevents invalid demand that a single factor carry both divisors; elicits the coprime multiplication warrant.

route.ask: Have you exhausted all allowed t? Which part of your reasoning would fail if you had only checked t=3,4,5?
route.why_this_ask: Tests the return from local examples to the universal quantifier, not merely copying the original worked proof.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: Core1A directly models n,n+1,n+2 and presents parity, residue cases and coprimality with explanations. This Core1B cycle begins by challenging the validity of finite evidence for an ending-at-t triple, requires a learner-written proof before reveal, then reconstructs each missing guarantee as a question tied to its teaching-step reference.

boundary_test.prompt: Suppose the claim changes to only TWO consecutive positive factors, (t−1)t, always being divisible by 6 for all integers t≥2. Is this universal claim true? Identify which guarantee from the three-factor proof fails. Record your boundary decision and reason before checking its answer. On a printed handout, write on a separate sheet.
boundary_test.answer: False. At t=2 the product is 1×2=2, which is not divisible by 6. Adjacent integers still guarantee an even factor but do NOT guarantee a multiple-of-three factor when there are only two, so the exhaustive three-residue argument no longer applies.
boundary_test.confirms: The learner recognizes that the proof depends on three consecutive factors, and can disprove a changed boundary with a specific counterexample rather than repeating the original answer.

questions.stem: For any positive integer n, show that n(n+1)(n+2) is divisible by 6. Explain why a few numerical checks do not establish the claim for every n.
conditions: The factors are three consecutive integers.

answer.summary: The product always contains a factor 2 and a factor 3; because these are coprime, 6 divides the product for every positive integer n.
reasoning: At least one of n and n+1 is even, since they are consecutive. Thus the whole product is divisible by 2.
For n modulo 3, check exactly the exhaustive cases 0, 1 and 2: the divisible factor is respectively n, n+2, and n+1. Thus the whole product is divisible by 3.
Since 2 and 3 are coprime and both divide the whole integer product, their product 6 also divides it.
Every positive integer belongs to one of these exhaustive parity/remainder cases. This proves a universal statement, whereas checking a few particular n only tests examples.
answer.check: For each n modulo 6 from 0 through 5, n(n+1)(n+2) is a multiple of 6; this exhaustive residue check independently corroborates the proof.

grade9v3:cognitive_demand.basis: The decisive task is a universal divisibility warrant for arbitrary integer m, not executing one numerical product.

grade9v3:analysis.stable_crux_move: Guarantee both a factor of two and a factor of three for every permissible starting m, then combine coprime divisors.
grade9v3:analysis.common_wrong_route: Check three sample m values or assert one chosen factor is always even and divisible by three.

questions.stem: A student checks m = 1, 2 and 3 and claims those examples prove that (m+1)(m+2)(m+3) is divisible by 6 for every positive integer m. Does that reasoning prove the universal claim? Decide, then construct a valid proof or counterexample for arbitrary positive m. Your argument must cover every m, not only tested values.
conditions: A few tested values are not accepted as a general proof.
This is original authored practice, not an SOF/NCERT exam item.

answer.summary: The three example checks do not prove the universal claim. However, the product is always divisible by 6: every three consecutive integers contain a factor of 2 and a factor of 3.
reasoning: The student's three checks do not prove a statement about every positive m; a valid argument must cover an arbitrary m.
Set n=m+1. Then the product is n(n+1)(n+2), and n is a positive integer.
At least one of n and n+1 is even, so 2 divides the product.
If n mod 3 is 0, 1 or 2, the factor n, n+2 or n+1 is divisible by 3 respectively, so 3 divides the product in every case.
The two coprime divisors 2 and 3 both divide the same product; therefore 6 divides it for every m.

reasoning_route.action: Reject the inference from three checked examples, then use n=m+1 to represent the factors as an arbitrary consecutive triple.
reasoning_route.why_valid: A finite collection of checks cannot establish a universal statement; for each positive m the substitution n=m+1 is valid and the consecutive-factor identity holds.

reasoning_route.action: Establish a factor of two from consecutive parity, not from tested values.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Adjacent integers have opposite parities, so one of n,n+1 is even for every n.

reasoning_route.action: Check the exhaustive three possible residues for n modulo 3 and combine the guaranteed coprime divisors.
reasoning_route.why_valid: The residues 0,1,2 exhaust all starts and ensure one factor divisible by 3, while parity independently gives factor 2. Coprimality licenses the product 6.

reasoning_route.action: Reverse-map n=m+1 and independently inspect each residue class modulo six as a check.
reasoning_route.why_valid: The identity maps back to the original arbitrary m; six exhaustive classes provide an independent arithmetic verification of the divisibility claim.
reasoning_route.output: same universal claim in m, with all residue classes checked

answer.check: For m congruent to any residue from 0 to 5 modulo 6, at least one of m+1,m+2,m+3 is even and one is divisible by 3. This corroborates, rather than replaces, the general proof.

scaffolds.text: Keep m arbitrary. Can a few checked examples establish a result for every m? State what a general proof must ensure.
What would it mean to guarantee divisibility of the whole product by 6? Identify the kind of general warrant you need, without deciding which factor provides it.
Do not assume one factor supplies every divisor. Can you make separate universal claims about two coprime divisor contributions, and verify that each applies to every start?

questions.stem: Let n be any positive integer. Prove, without testing only particular numbers, that n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)(n+4) is always divisible by 120. Explain why a proof using the first four factors alone is incomplete.
conditions: n is an arbitrary positive integer.
You may use the earlier established result that any four consecutive positive integers have a product divisible by 24.
You must independently justify the additional factor that makes 120; numerical examples alone are insufficient.
This is independently authored practice, not an SOF source question.

answer.summary: The first four consecutive factors have product divisible by 24. Of the five factors, one is divisible by 5. As gcd(24,5)=1, the full product is divisible by 120 for every positive integer n.
reasoning: Let P=n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)(n+4), for an arbitrary positive integer n.
The four consecutive factors n through n+3 form a product divisible by 24, by the established four-factor result. Therefore 24 divides P.
Exactly one of n,n+1,n+2,n+3,n+4 is congruent to 0 modulo 5, so 5 divides P for every possible n.
Because gcd(24,5)=1, the simultaneous divisibility of P by 24 and by 5 implies 120 divides P. The multiple of five may occur among the first four factors; this does not invalidate the conclusion.
Checking selected n values would not prove the universal statement. The four-factor warrant plus all five residue positions covers every positive integer.

reasoning_route.action: Name the product P of five consecutive integers with arbitrary positive start n.
reasoning_route.why_valid: The notation covers every permitted positive integer n.

reasoning_route.action: Apply the previously established 24-divisibility theorem to the first four factors.
reasoning_route.why_valid: n,n+1,n+2,n+3 are any four consecutive positive integers, so their product and hence P are multiples of 24.

reasoning_route.action: Prove that exactly one of the five consecutive integers is divisible by 5, then combine coprime divisors 24 and 5.
reasoning_route.why_valid: The residues n mod 5 = 0,1,2,3,4 exhaust all positive starts. In each case one of five consecutive factors is a multiple of 5, and gcd(24,5)=1.

reasoning_route.action: Check a complete set of residue classes modulo 120 only as a corroboration, not as isolated examples.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Each positive integer is represented by one of the 120 residue classes, providing an independent exhaustive check.

answer.check: For each residue r from 0 to 119, the integer r(r+1)(r+2)(r+3)(r+4) has remainder zero modulo 120. This is an exhaustive modular check, not a list of sample values.
